<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning with
<br class="ltx_break">Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">World models learned from high-dimensional visual observations allow agents to make decisions and plan directly in latent space, avoiding pixel-level reconstruction. However, recent latent predictive architectures (JEPAs), including the DINO world model (DINO-WM), display a degradation in test time robustness due to their sensitivity to “slow features”. These include visual variations such as background changes and distractors that are irrelevant to the task being solved. We address this limitation by augmenting the predictive objective with a bisimulation encoder that enforces control-relevant state equivalence, mapping states with similar transition dynamics to nearby latent states while limiting contributions from slow features. We evaluate our model on a simple navigation task under different test-time background changes and visual distractors. Across all benchmarks, our model consistently improves robustness to slow features while operating in a reduced latent space, up to <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller than that of DINO-WM. Moreover, our model is agnostic to the choice of pretrained visual encoder and maintains robustness when paired with DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT features.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Constructing spatial and temporal models of the world to predict future outcomes and guide decisions is a crucial capability of the human brain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 2012</a>)</cite>. In machine learning, this is mirrored through world models that are learned from high-dimensional visual observations, enabling efficient prediction, planning, and control by reasoning over learned latent dynamics rather than raw sensory inputs. Planning with such a “compressed” representation of the environment dynamics has become a cornerstone of contemporary robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, model-based reinforcement learning (RL), and control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebert et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thuruthel et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Matsuo et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khorrambakht et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as it provides data efficiency and generalization across tasks while avoiding online interaction and visual reconstruction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">An impactful line of recent work centers on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), which eschew reconstruction of raw observations in favor of learning representations by predicting future latent embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grill et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caron et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assran et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balestriero and LeCun, 2025</a>)</cite>. Building on JEPAs, the DINO world model (DINO-WM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> learns a latent predictive dynamic by encoding visual observations through a pretrained DINOv2 feature extractor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. This yields zero-shot planning, with a pretrained, reward-free world model on entirely new tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their empirical success, JEPAs suffer from a fundamental limitation: they pay too much attention to <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">slowly changing</em> and <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task-irrelevant features</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. These slow features refer to aspects of the raw observations that change gradually over time, but are irrelevant for planning, such as background textures, lighting, camera viewpoints, and distractors. In the presence of slow features, the predictive objective in JEPA can be minimized by encoding <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> such temporally consistent information, yielding degenerate solutions. As a result, world models trained under fixed visual conditions often fail to generalize when the background changes at test time (despite identical underlying object dynamics). This limitation has been discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2022</a>)</cite> for JEPAs and empirically observed to be true for DINO-WM (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Right)).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, this limitation <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cannot</em> be fully resolved by larger visual foundation models alone (such as DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, SimDINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, iBOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, masked autoencoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, among others) as they also extract control-irrelevant information. Even with invariant perception modules, the learned latent dynamics may still entangle control-relevant states with nuisance visual features, leading to brittle planning under visual distribution shifts at test time. Ideally, a world model should encode only those aspects of the state that are relevant for predicting future states, while being invariant to task-irrelevant visual factors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:317.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F0F0F0;">
<span id="S1.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question.</span> Can we learn latent world models that retain the joint-embedding predictive strengths while also being robust to the slow features?</span>
</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We address this question using bisimulation metrics for learning invariant representations on top of pretrained visual feature extractors (i.e., DINOv2, SimDINOv2, iBOT). These metrics define state equivalences based on immediate rewards and transition dynamics, and have been studied as a principled foundation for state abstraction in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferns et al., 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, transfer learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro and Precup, 2010</a>)</cite>, and invariant representation learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kemertas and Aumentado-Armstrong, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tkachev and Abate, 2011</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>. By construction, encoders trained with a bisimulation regularizer discard nuisance features that do not affect control, making it a natural candidate for addressing the slow-feature limitation of JEPAs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:317.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;">
<span id="S1.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Key Point.</span> DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> displays a substantial degradation in performance on relatively simple navigation tasks (e.g., PointMaze <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2020</a>)</cite>) when evaluated under background changes and visual distractors at test time (see Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Right)). To address this, we propose a <em id="S1.p7.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bisimulation encoder</em> for visual world models that augments latent dynamics with an on-policy bisimulation objective, enforcing invariance in the learned latent space. The bisimulation encoder is trained jointly with the transition model, enforcing states with similar transition behavior to be mapped to nearby latent embeddings while discarding task-irrelevant visual information (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Importantly, we also show that explicit reward prediction is not fundamental to learning invariant world-model representations, thereby simplifying training.</span>
</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/encoding_motivation.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/269;" width="429" height="269" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Visually distinct observations that differ only in background (checkerboard and gradient) are first mapped to latent embeddings <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> by a pretrained encoder (initial state in green, goal in red). A bisimulation encoder then projects these into lower-dimensional representations <math id="S1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.F1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, which are equivalent under on-policy transition dynamics. In contrast, an observation with different underlying dynamics is mapped to <math id="S1.F1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and separated in the bisimulation space.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span> Our main contributions are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> We propose a bisimulation encoder for visual world models that enforces control-relevant state equivalence while discarding task-irrelevant visual features from pretrained visual feature extractors (e.g., DINOv2, SimDINOv2, iBOT).
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> We integrate the bisimulation objective into a latent predictive world model architecture (see Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Left)), showing that invariant representations can be learned jointly with the transition model <em id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">without</em> relying on reward prediction.
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="S1.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> We show that our bisimulation encoder yields robust planning performance under several background changes and a moving distractor for a navigation task, with latent embeddings dimensions that are <math id="S1.p9.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller than DINO-WM. 
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="S1.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> We validate our model with three different pretrained visual encoder backbones: DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT, namely, and show consistent robustness over slow features when compared to DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> both with and without domain randomization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tobin et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<table id="S1.F2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<td id="S1.F2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:-5pt 2.0pt;">  <img src="2602.18639v1/figures/motivating_pointmaze.png" id="S1.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:205/120;" width="205" height="120" alt="Refer to caption"></td>
<td id="S1.F2.2.1.3" class="ltx_td" style="padding:-5pt 2.0pt;"></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left.</span> Model architecture and training objectives. Visual observations are encoded using a frozen pretrained visual encoder, followed by a bisimulation encoder that maps features into a low-dimensional, control-relevant latent space. The bisimulation loss is trained jointly with the latent transition model, enforcing invariance to task-irrelevant visual features. <span id="S1.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right.</span> Rollouts for PointMaze navigation under a background change at test time. For clarity, the background change is not depicted in the figure. See Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Background Changes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> for details on background changes. While DINO-WM fails to reach the goal due to background change our model succeeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs).</span>
Joint embedding predictive architectures learn feature representations by predicting future latent states rather than reconstructing observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grill et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caron et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assran et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balestriero and LeCun, 2025</a>)</cite>. Most relevant to our work is DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> that learns latent dynamics directly in the space of pretrained DINOv2 visual features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, avoiding pixel-level reconstruction. However, latent prediction in DINO-WM remains sensitive to slow, control-irrelevant features. We address this limitation by augmenting the predictive objective with a bisimulation encoder to enforce control-relevant invariances.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bisimulation metrics and invariant representations.</span> Bisimulation provides a principled way of behavioral equivalence in MDPs by quantifying approximate equivalence through reward discrepancies and mismatches in future state distributions for different states under the same policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferns et al., 2011</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abate, 2013</a>)</cite>. Most relevant to our work is BS-MPC in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>, which incorporates a bisimulation metric loss for model predictive control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kouvaritakis and Cannon, 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lenz et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. In contrast to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>, we leverage bisimulation metrics to “filter out” control-irrelevant information from a pretrained feature space (e.g., that of DINOv2, SimDINOv2, iBOT). Moreover, we jointly train our prediction model without relying on reward prediction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model-based control with latent world models.</span>
Model-based RL with world models enable planning by rolling out learned dynamics in a compact latent space, which has been effective for high-dimensional tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. In robotics, latent dynamics models are commonly paired with sampling-based optimizers for action selection, including the cross-entropy method (CEM), which is widely used for planning with learned world models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rubinstein and Kroese, 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Our control stack follows this line, we plan with CEM with the learned latent dynamics, and focus on the representation learning side, i.e., how to learn a latent space that is robust to slow features so that planning remains reliable under visual distribution shifts in test time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now introduce the notation and preliminaries on JEPAs, bisimulation metrics, and invariant representation learning. Throughout, we consider a vision-based control task given by a partially observable MDP (POMDP) that evolves in discrete time <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\left\{0,1,2,\dots\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\left\{0,1,2,\dots\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>. An observation is an RGB image <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>, an action is denoted by <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a trajectory is a sequence <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1},a_{t+1},\dots\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1},a_{t+1},\dots\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote the data distribution induced by a behavior policy <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, meaning that <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> when rollouts are generated by playing the environment with <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. We use <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\cdot\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\cdot\right]</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the expectation with respect to this data distribution.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">JEPAs learn a visual encoder <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}:\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}:\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> that maps an observation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to a latent embedding, i.e., <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}},</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{z}</annotation></semantics></math> is the embedding dimension and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is the vector of encoder parameters. Jointly, a predictor (i.e., latent dynamics model) <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{T}_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{T}_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> is trained to map the current latent state and action to a predicted next latent state <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{z}_{t+1}=\tilde{T}_{\phi}\left(z_{t},a_{t}\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{z}_{t+1}=\tilde{T}_{\phi}\left(z_{t},a_{t}\right),</annotation></semantics></math> with parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since representations are defined up to arbitrary invertible transformations, JEPA training includes a target embedding.
The target is denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The JEPA objective minimizes the prediction loss between <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{z}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{z}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}\left(\theta,\phi\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\ell\left(\tilde{T}_{\phi}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right),a_{t}\right),f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)\right)\right],\vskip-5.69046pt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>pred</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}\left(\theta,\phi\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\ell\left(\tilde{T}_{\phi}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right),a_{t}\right),f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)\right)\right],\vskip-5.69046pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean squared error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasize that DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, follow this principle, with the key distinction that the visual encoder parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> are fixed and not learned during training. Therefore, observations are first mapped to latent embeddings using a pretrained visual foundation model (e.g., DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>), and a predictive dynamics model is trained on top of that latent space. Here, we also treat the pretrained visual encoder as fixed and train an extra bisimulation encoder jointly with the dynamics on top of it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Remark 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> </span>(Slow Features)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasize that JEPAs inadvertently focus on the slow features. In particular, when observations contain static backgrounds or persistent distractors that vary slowly relative to task-relevant dynamics, the prediction loss (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) can be minimized by encoding such features into the latent embedding <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, since they induce small temporal differences <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|z_{t+1}-z_{t}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|z_{t+1}-z_{t}\|</annotation></semantics></math>. As a result, slowly varying nuisance information may dominate the predictive objective, leading to latent embeddings that fail to capture the underlying task structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and thus are not generalizable to background changes at test time (see Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Right)). This limitation motivates the use of bisimulation. By defining latent distances in terms of on-policy transition behavior, bisimulation induces representations that collapse nuisance visual features while preserving the task-relevant information for planning.</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Bisimulation Metric</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let us now (informally) revisit the definition of on-policy bisimulation metrics from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro, 2020</a>)</cite>. Intuitively, two latent states, in the pretrained visual encoder space, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> are “bisimilar” if they induce similar immediate rewards (for optimality equivalence) and similar future state evolution (for dynamics equivalence) under the same actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, the environment is partially observed and represented through latent embeddings obtained from a visual encoder (e.g., DINOv2, SimDINOv2, iBOT). The goal is to learn a lower-dimensional representation <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=h_{\eta}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=h_{\eta}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{w}\ll d_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>≪</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{w}\ll d_{z}</annotation></semantics></math>, that preserves control-relevant structure while discarding nuisance visual variation. We formalize state equivalence with the <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">on-policy</em> bisimulation metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3.2</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(On-Policy Bisimulation Metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro, 2020</a>)</cite>)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, a reward function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(z,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(z,a)</annotation></semantics></math>, and a transition kernel <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z)</annotation></semantics></math> induced by <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, the on-policy bisimulation metric is</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})=\underbrace{\left|r_{\pi}(z)-r_{\pi}(z^{\prime})\right|}_{\mathrm{reward~similarity}}+\gamma\underbrace{W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right)}_{\mathrm{dynamics~similarity}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mrow><mi>reward</mi><mo lspace="0.270em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>similarity</mi></mrow></munder><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>W</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>(</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mrow><mi>dynamics</mi><mo lspace="0.270em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>similarity</mi></mrow></munder></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})=\underbrace{\left|r_{\pi}(z)-r_{\pi}(z^{\prime})\right|}_{\mathrm{reward~similarity}}+\gamma\underbrace{W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right)}_{\mathrm{dynamics~similarity}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="r_{\pi}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid z)}[r(z,a)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\pi}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid z)}[r(z,a)]</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> is a discount factor, and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>-Wasserstein distance.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:317.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;">
<span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">On Dropping the Reward Term.</span> Note that <math id="S3.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">d</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> has two terms: a reward similarity term <math id="S3.SS2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lvert r_{\pi}(z)-r_{\pi}(z^{\prime})\rvert" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">r</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">r</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lvert r_{\pi}(z)-r_{\pi}(z^{\prime})\rvert</annotation></semantics></math> and a dynamics similarity term measured via the <math id="S3.SS2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>-Wasserstein distance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Givens and Shortt, 1984</a>)</cite>. The reward term ensures that if two state trajectories are similar, they are not collapsed if they yield different rewards. In particular, such reward discrepancy is crucial when bisimulation is used for policy transfer or value-function approximation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferns et al., 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro et al., 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro and Precup, 2010</a>)</cite>. However, for the purpose of learning an invariant representation for JEPAs, we claim that this term is not fundamental. This is because the transition term alone induces a meaningful notion of equivalence: states that exhibit similar evolution under the same action sequences are mapped to nearby representations in the bisimulation latent space (see the illustration in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>)</span>
</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, dropping the reward term is well aligned with JEPAs, which are inherently reward-free and focus on predictive consistency in latent space. Incorporating rewards would require task-specific supervision and would break the modularity between representation learning and zero-shot downstream planning. Accordingly, we omit the reward term in our implementation and rely only on approximating the Wasserstein transition similarity to enforce invariance. This design choice is further supported numerically in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, where a reward predictor is included.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Learning Invariant Representations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Now, we discuss the invariant representation learning problem for our joint-embedding predictive world model. Recall that <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> typically contains both control-relevant information and nuisance features. Our goal is to learn an encoder <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}},</annotation></semantics></math> that limits the contribution of the slow features in the transition dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To do so, we jointly learn the dynamics in the bisimulation space through
<math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}},</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{t+1}=T_{\phi}\left(w_{t},a_{t}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{t+1}=T_{\phi}\left(w_{t},a_{t}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> predicts the next latent state. With the notation set up in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we have the predictive dynamics augmented with the bisimulation encoder, i.e., <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\phi}(h_{\eta}(f_{\theta}(o_{t})),a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\phi}(h_{\eta}(f_{\theta}(o_{t})),a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where again <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To connect invariance to bisimulation, we consider an abstract state space <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}}</annotation></semantics></math> equipped with the metric <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>. We aim to learn <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\eta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\eta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> jointly so that the distances in <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}</annotation></semantics></math> approximate an on-policy bisimulation metric, meaning that states that are equivalent for control under rollouts are mapped nearby in such latent space. We do this by optimizing a bisimulation objective that aligns pairwise latent distances with a target quantity that compares on-policy dynamics. Concretely, for a pair of observation, action, and next observation <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(o_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(o^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t},o^{\prime}_{t+1}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(o^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t},o^{\prime}_{t+1}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> drawn from <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have the latent states</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

latents}},\;\underbrace{w_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z_{t}\right),\;w^{\prime}_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z^{\prime}_{t}\right)}_{\text{Bisimulation latents}}.\vskip-5.69046pt" display="block" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Pretrained latents</mtext></munder><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Bisimulation latents</mtext></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation latents}},\;\underbrace{w_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z_{t}\right),\;w^{\prime}_{t}=h_{\eta}\left(z^{\prime}_{t}\right)}_{\text{Bisimulation latents}}.\vskip-5.69046pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The transition dynamics <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> is trained using</p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\hskip-2.84544pt\left[\left\|h_{\eta}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)\right)\hskip-1.42271pt-\hskip-1.42271ptT_{\phi}\left(h_{\eta}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\right),a_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\right]\hskip-1.42271pt," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>dyn</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em"
