encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\hskip-2.84544pt\left[\left\|h_{\eta}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t+1}\right)\right)\hskip-1.42271pt-\hskip-1.42271ptT_{\phi}\left(h_{\eta}\left(f_{\theta}\left(o_{t}\right)\right),a_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\right]\hskip-1.42271pt,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">and we note that, in practice, as we do not have <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute the empirical mean instead (i.e., MSE).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, for invariance, our loss encourages the distance <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|w_{t}-w^{\prime}_{t}\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|w_{t}-w^{\prime}_{t}\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to match a control-relevant similarity signal measured by the bisimulation metric. We define the on-policy one-step bisimulation target between states as <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{bisim}}(\eta,\phi)\triangleq\gamma\left\|T_{\phi}\left(w_{t},a_{t}\right)-T_{\phi}\left(w^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t}\right)\right\|_{2}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{bisim}}(\eta,\phi)\triangleq\gamma\left\|T_{\phi}\left(w_{t},a_{t}\right)-T_{\phi}\left(w^{\prime}_{t},a^{\prime}_{t}\right)\right\|_{2},</annotation></semantics></math>
where it compares the predicted next latent states under the learned dynamics. We fit the bisimulation encoder by minimizing</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\left(\left\|w_{t}-w^{\prime}_{t}\right\|_{2}-\Delta_{\mathrm{bisim}}(\eta,\phi)\right)^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\pi}}\left[\left(\left\|w_{t}-w^{\prime}_{t}\right\|_{2}-\Delta_{\mathrm{bisim}}(\eta,\phi)\right)^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Finally, we define the overall training objective as</p>
<table id="S3.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hskip-9.95863pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{jepa-bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{bisim}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>jepa</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>bisim</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>dyn</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hskip-9.95863pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{jepa-bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\left(\eta,\phi\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{bisim}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bisim}}\left(\eta,\phi\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.3" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{bisim}}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>bisim</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{bisim}}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> being the regularization weight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Minimizing the loss formalizes our goal of learning a compact latent space that preserves on-policy predictive structure for planning while suppressing task-irrelevant visual features. We next describe the architecture, loss instantiation, and planning in the learned bisimulation space.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Our World Model</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe our architecture for learning invariant world models that builds on pretrained visual features (DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT) and augments them with a bisimulation encoder to suppress task-irrelevant information. The model learns latent transition dynamics and performs planning via MPC with CEM. An overview of the full pipeline and training objectives is shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Left).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Pretrained Visual Encoders</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our experiments, we consider three self-supervised visual encoders: DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (with ViT-S/14), SimDINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (with ViT-B/16), and iBOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (with ViT-S/16). These are trained on large-scale image datasets using joint embedding or masked prediction objectives and have been shown to produce semantically rich visual features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These visual encoders are <em id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">patch-based</em>, namely,
<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of patches. Most importantly, they are trained without access to the transition dynamics, actions and/or rewards, and thus capture <em id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generic</em> visual features rather than control-relevant structure. In particular, they are not tailored for planning and are not fine-tuned to allow for visual shifts in test time. Our goal is to adapt their feature embeddings by learning an additional bisimulation encoder on top of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{z_{t}\}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{z_{t}\}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (see Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-(Left)).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When using DINOv2 features, we refer to our model as DINO-Bisim. Similarly, we use SimDINO-Bisim and iBOT-Bisim when paired with SimDINOv2 and iBOT visual feature extractors, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Bisimulation Encoder</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given pretrained visual embeddings <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we learn a bisimulation encoder
<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\eta}:\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{z}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{w}},w_{t}=h_{\eta}(z_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\eta}:\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{z}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d_{w}},w_{t}=h_{\eta}(z_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math> as discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. We note that in contrast to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>, our bisimulation encoder is designed in patches (we refer the reader to Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1.SSS3" title="A.1.3 Patch design in Bisimulation Model ‣ A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1.3</span></a> for details). Such encoder consists of a per-patch residual MLP projection head (Linear-ResMLP-Linear) that maps each DINOv2 patch embedding (or raw image patch) into a <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{w}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{w}=32</annotation></semantics></math> dimensional latent, followed by learned spatial positional embeddings and LayerNorm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This encoder is trained to ensure that distances in the <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>-space reflect on-policy bisimulation distances, as defined in (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.3 Learning Invariant Representations ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). To this end, we <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">flatten</em> the spatial patch features prior to computing the previously defined losses and compare states across different trajectories that are stored in a <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">replay buffer</em>, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. However, minimizing the bisimulation loss admits degenerate solutions as mapping all states to a single representation trivially minimizes pairwise distances, and we refer to this as the representation <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">collapse</em>. To circumvent such collapse, prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bardes et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> has adopted variance-invariance-covariance regularization (VICReg) to guarantee that each latent dimension keeps sufficient variance over batches of states. We refer the reader to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bardes et al., 2021</a>, Section 4.1)</cite> for an excellent overview of the approach. Here, invariance is given by the bisimulation loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In our setting, however, the standard VICReg <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bardes et al., 2021</a>)</cite> <em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">may be</em> insufficient. This is because, for the pretrained visual encoders considered in this work (i.e., DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT) a large fraction of the variance is often concentrated in a small number of principal components that correlate with the slow features rather than task-relevant dynamics. Therefore, by imposing a uniform variance across all coordinates may preserve nuisance visual features, preventing the bisimulation encoder from collapsing the task-irrelevant information (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Leveraging this insight, we propose a PCA-based VCReg loss, which adapts VICReg to pretrained visual embeddings by guaranteeing a minimum variance in directions that are not dominated by a large fraction of slow features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/pca_pointmaze.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/126;" width="452" height="126" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>First principal component (PC1) of latent embeddings produced by different visual feature encoders for a PointMaze observation. In all cases, PC1 captures a large percentage of the total variance and predominantly encodes background and layout information rather than control-relevant features, motivating our PCA-based VICReg in the bisimulation encoder.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the pretrained visual embeddings from DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT, allocate a large amount of variance to the first principal component (PC1), which are correlated with task-irrelevant features coming from backgrounds and distractors. If we use the standard VICReg loss with uniform variance across the coordinates of the bisimulation latent space, the optimizer may still preserve such irrelevant directions simply to satisfy the variance threshold, conflicting with the goal of learning a representation invariant to those slow features.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we do VICReg in the PCA basis of the current batch. Let
<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{c}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}(w_{1}-\bar{w})^{\top}&amp;\ldots&amp;(w_{B}-\bar{w})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt"><mtr><mtd><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mtd><mtd><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mtd><mtd><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{c}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}(w_{1}-\bar{w})^{\top}&amp;\ldots&amp;(w_{B}-\bar{w})^{\top}\end{bmatrix},</annotation></semantics></math>
be the matrix with centered embeddings in the batch of size <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{w}</annotation></semantics></math> is the average. We define the empirical covariance <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\triangleq\frac{W_{c}^{\top}W_{c}}{B-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>≜</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\triangleq\frac{W_{c}^{\top}W_{c}}{B-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and further compute its eigendecomposition as <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma=U\Lambda U^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma=U\Lambda U^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d_{w}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d_{w}})</annotation></semantics></math>. We extract the PCA coordinates <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}_{b}=U^{\top}(w_{b}-\bar{w})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}_{b}=U^{\top}(w_{b}-\bar{w})</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> be the batch matrix with rows <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}_{b}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>b</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}_{b}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To construct the PCA-based VICReg loss, we only enforce the variance floor on the tail PCs, namely indices <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\{i_{0},\ldots,d_{w}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\{i_{0},\ldots,d_{w}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is a cutoff index (e.g., <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{0}=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{0}=2</annotation></semantics></math>). Let <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{i}\triangleq\sigma_{\min}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}+\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{i}\triangleq\sigma_{\min}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}+\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math> and write the variance term</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}var}}(\eta)\triangleq\frac{1}{d_{w}-i_{0}+1}\sum_{i=i_{0}}^{d_{w}}\left[\max\left(0,\kappa_{i}\right)\right]^{2}.\vskip-5.69046pt" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>pca</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>var</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}var}}(\eta)\triangleq\frac{1}{d_{w}-i_{0}+1}\sum_{i=i_{0}}^{d_{w}}\left[\max\left(0,\kappa_{i}\right)\right]^{2}.\vskip-5.69046pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> is a small constant for numerical stability and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a minimum standard deviation. On the other hand, we regularize cross-covariances as</p>
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
