<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\Sigma}_{pq}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\Sigma}_{pq}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(p,q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p,q)</annotation></semantics></math> entry of the covariance in PCs coordinates, namely, the covariance matrix <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\Sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\Sigma}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we combine the two PCA-based terms</p>
<table id="S4.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}vc}}(\eta)\triangleq\alpha_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}var}}(\eta)+\alpha_{\mathrm{c}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}cov}}(\eta)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>pca</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>vc</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>pca</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>var</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>pca</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>cov</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}vc}}(\eta)\triangleq\alpha_{\mathrm{v}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}var}}(\eta)+\alpha_{\mathrm{c}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pca\text{-}cov}}(\eta),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">with weights <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\mathrm{v}},\alpha_{\mathrm{c}}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\mathrm{v}},\alpha_{\mathrm{c}}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, to the predictive loss (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.3 Learning Invariant Representations ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We refer the reader to Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> for details on how the PCA-based VICReg loss is implemented and empirical evidence on how it helps the representation collapse while keeping control-relevant features. We emphasize that if the visual encoder does not isolate control-irrelevant features within a dominant principal component, the PCA-based VICReg regularization becomes <em id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">optional</em>. In this case, the bisimulation-based encoder alone can mitigate, though only partially, the influence of task-irrelevant variations in the learned representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S4.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:317.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;">
<span id="S4.SS3.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">On the PCA-based VICReg.</span> By not enforcing a minimum variance on the leading PCA components <math id="S4.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i&lt;i_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">&lt;</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">i</mi><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i&lt;i_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the bisimulation encoder can collapse the directions that are dominated by slow features, which concentrate in the top components of the pretrained features. At the same time, enforcing a variance floor on the tail components <math id="S4.SS3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\geq i_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">≥</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">i</mi><mn style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\geq i_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> prevents <math id="S4.SS3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S4.SS3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\equiv\mathrm{constant}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">≡</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">constant</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\equiv\mathrm{constant}</annotation></semantics></math> and ensures that the representation retains sufficient diversity to separate control-relevant states. The covariance loss further yields information to be spread across coordinates.</span>
</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation.</span> Our bisimulation encoder is initialized with random parameters and is first trained using the standard VICReg objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bardes et al., 2021</a>)</cite> for a small number of epochs (<math id="S4.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>) to stabilize representation learning. We then perform a one-time principal component analysis to identify the dominant direction associated with task-irrelevant information. After <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> (to be set by the practitioner) epochs, we replace the standard VICReg loss with the PCA-based one, which helps to suppresses the additional variance along the identified principal component directions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Transition Model</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We model latent dynamics using a vision transformer that predicts the next state in the bisimulation latent space. Following DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the vision transformer architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy, 2020</a>)</cite> is suitable for processing the underlying patch-based embeddings. Since the bisimulation latent states are already represented as sequences of patch embeddings, we remove the ViT tokenization layer, yielding a decoder-only transformer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The transition model takes as input a history of past bisimulation latent states and actions across multiple trajectories, <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{\left(w_{j,t-H:t-1},a_{j,t-H:t-1}\right)\}_{j=1}^{N_{\text{traj}}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>traj</mtext></msub></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\left(w_{j,t-H:t-1},a_{j,t-H:t-1}\right)\}_{j=1}^{N_{\text{traj}}},</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the context length and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{traj}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>traj</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{traj}}</annotation></semantics></math> the number of trajectories, and it predicts the next latent state <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., in the bisimulation space). Note that the subscript <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the trajectory embedding and action at time step <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To respect temporal causality, a causal attention mask is implemented (as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) ensuring that predictions at time <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> depend only on past latent states and actions. More precisely, each patch embedding <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> attends to the corresponding patch embeddings <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{w_{t-H:t-1}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{p}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{w_{t-H:t-1}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{p}}</annotation></semantics></math> over the context. Predicting all patches jointly yields global spatial structure and temporal dynamics that improves temporal generalization as discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">By “filtering out” task-irrelevant visual features, the bisimulation encoder enables the transition model to learn dynamics that are invariant. The learned joint-embedding predictive world model is then used for planning via MPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kouvaritakis and Cannon, 2016</a>)</cite>, with actions selected using the cross-entropy method (CEM).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Planning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The MPC approach selects the actions whose predicted latent rollouts reach a desired goal observation. That is, given an initial observation <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and a goal observation <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>, our model will first compute their latents through the pretrained visual and bisimulation encoders,</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}=f_{\theta}(o_{0}),\;z_{g}=f_{\theta}(o_{g}),\;w_{0}=h_{\eta}(z_{0}),\;w_{g}=h_{\eta}(z_{g})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}=f_{\theta}(o_{0}),\;z_{g}=f_{\theta}(o_{g}),\;w_{0}=h_{\eta}(z_{0}),\;w_{g}=h_{\eta}(z_{g})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Starting from <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the transition model is used to rollout predicted states under a candidate action sequence <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{a_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{a_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\hat{w}_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}=T_{\phi}(\hat{w}_{t},\{a_{t}\}_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\hat{w}_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}=T_{\phi}(\hat{w}_{t},\{a_{t}\}_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{0}=w_{0}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{0}=w_{0}.</annotation></semantics></math> Planning is then cast as minimizing a terminal cost that is the difference between the predicted final latent state and the goal latent state,</p>
<table id="S4.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle c(w_{T},\{a_{t}\}_{t})=\left\|\hat{w}_{T}(\{a_{t}\}_{t})-w_{g}\right\|^{2}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle c(w_{T},\{a_{t}\}_{t})=\left\|\hat{w}_{T}(\{a_{t}\}_{t})-w_{g}\right\|^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">For brevity, we omit the explicit dependence on the action sequence and write <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c(w_{T})=\left\|\hat{w}_{T}-w_{g}\right\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(w_{T})=\left\|\hat{w}_{T}-w_{g}\right\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>A Generalization Bound</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before turning to the experiments, we also provide a theoretical justification for learning bisimulation-based representations on top of JEPA latents. Let us first define the <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-step on-policy cost-to-go as follows:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex8"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046ptJ_{T}^{\pi}(z)\triangleq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}{\small\gamma^{t}c\left(h_{\eta}(z_{t})\right)\mid z_{0}=z}\right],\;z_{t+1}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">γ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msup><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">h</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">η</mi></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">z</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">z</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">z</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046ptJ_{T}^{\pi}(z)\triangleq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}{\small\gamma^{t}c\left(h_{\eta}(z_{t})\right)\mid z_{0}=z}\right],\;z_{t+1}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where the expectation is taken over trajectories <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{z_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{z_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> induced by policy <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and transition kernel <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> starting from a visual pretrained latent state <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}=z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}=z</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.1</span></span><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Reward-free planning generalization bound)<span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\eta}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\eta}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>-approximately preserves the reward-free bisimulation metric in the sense that</span></p>
<table id="S4.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left|\left\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\right\|_{2}-d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})\right|\leq\varepsilon,\;\text{ for any }z,z^{\prime}.\vskip-1.42271pt" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> for any </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\left\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\right\|_{2}-d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})\right|\leq\varepsilon,\;\text{ for any }z,z^{\prime}.\vskip-1.42271pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In addition, suppose that <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\eta}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\eta}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is uniformly bounded as <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|h_{\eta}(z)\right\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|h_{\eta}(z)\right\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and thus <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|w_{g}\right\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|w_{g}\right\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then for any two pretrained visual latent embeddings <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z,z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z,z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex10"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left|J_{T}^{\pi}(z)-J_{T}^{\pi}(z^{\prime})\right|\leq 8{H}_{w}Td_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left|J_{T}^{\pi}(z)-J_{T}^{\pi}(z^{\prime})\right|\leq 8{H}_{w}Td_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We defer the proof of this result to Appendix <a href="#A1.SS8" title="A.8 Reward-Free Generalization Bound: Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also note that the linear dependence on the horizon <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> contrasts with the <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1-\gamma^{T})/(1-\gamma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1-\gamma^{T})/(1-\gamma)</annotation></semantics></math> dependence from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>. This difference arises from dropping the reward term in the bisimulation metric: while reward-aware bisimulation enables geometric discounting of cost discrepancies through immediate reward alignment, a reward-free metric propagates the discrepancies through the transition dynamics, yielding a cumulative horizon-dependent bound. In this sense, the <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> factor can be interpreted as the price paid for enforcing control-relevant invariance without task-specific reward supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S4.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:317.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;">
<span id="S4.SS6.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS6.p4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Key Takeaway.</span> The above result implies that if two latent states in the pretrained visual encoder space differ only due to nuisance visual variations, such as slow features, then their induced planning behavior remains similar. More concretely, let <math id="S4.SS6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=f_{\theta}(o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">f</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">o</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=f_{\theta}(o)</annotation></semantics></math> embed a PointMaze scene with a checkerboard background, and let <math id="S4.SS6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}=f_{\theta}(o^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">f</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">o</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}=f_{\theta}(o^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> embed the same scene with a gradient background (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), since these visual changes do not affect on-policy transition behavior, the bisimulation distance <math id="S4.SS6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">d</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> is small. Consequently, the difference in the induced planning cost is bounded by <math id="S4.SS6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}\left(d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})\,T\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">d</mi><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">z</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">T</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}\left(d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})\,T\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, robustness of planning when starting from <math id="S4.SS6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.SS6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">w</mi><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5FF;" mathbackground="#F5F5FF">′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> in the bisimulation latent space is governed by their distance in that space.</span>
</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now evaluate our world model. Our experiments assess robustness to slow, task-irrelevant visual features, such as background changes and distractors, and isolate their impact on the planning performance. We compare our model to DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and domain randomization (DR) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tobin et al., 2017</a>)</cite> for a simple navigation task under different visual conditions, and pretrained visual encoders.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>A Simple Navigation Task</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our model on a simple navigation task: the MuJoCo PointMaze <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. This is commonly used as benchmark for goal-conditioned planning and navigation from visual observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sobal et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parthasarathy et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Despite its simplicity, PointMaze provides a controlled setting to assess robustness to background changes and distractors, while keeping the transition dynamics fixed. Further details on the task setup are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Additional Information on the Navigation Task ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although PointMaze is a fairly simple navigation task, we observe that DINO-WM has a substantial drop in the performance under test-time background changes and moving distractors. This highlights that even for a simple task, sensitivity to slow features can negatively impact planning, motivating the need for an invariant latent representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metric.</span> We report performance using the success rate (SR), defined as the fraction of successful episodes over <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> independently sampled initial and goal pairs. An episode is considered successful if the agent approximately reaches the goal region within a fixed number of steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Baseline</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our model with two baselines: DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and domain DR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tobin et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Both baselines are evaluated under the same task, planning horizon, and evaluation metric previously described.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DINO-WM.</span> We use the original DINO-WM architecture as proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The model operates directly on pretrained DINOv2 patch embeddings with <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>196</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196</annotation></semantics></math> patches, each of dimensionality <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>384</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">384</annotation></semantics></math>, and learns latent dynamics without explicit invariance regularization. DINO-WM is trained with a batch size of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Domain Randomization (DR).</span> We also train DINO-WM with domain randomization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tobin et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. In particular, we randomize the visual appearance of the task for <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the training dataset by applying background color changes and gradient-based background modifications, for the PointMaze task. To avoid introducing spurious temporal artifacts, the randomized background is kept consistent across trajectories. We refer the reader to Appendix <a href="#A1.SS5" title="A.5 Domain Randomization for the PointMaze Task ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our model adopts the same number of visual patches (i.e., <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>196</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196</annotation></semantics></math>) as DINO-WM, but introduce a bisimulation encoder that maps each patch to a <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional latent embedding (see Figure <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.1.3 Patch design in Bisimulation Model ‣ A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). This leads to a latent space that is <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower-dimensional than the <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>384</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">384</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional patch embeddings used by DINO-WM. Our model is trained with a batch size of <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math>. We refer the reader to Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1.SSS4" title="A.1.4 Hyperparameters ‣ A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1.4</span></a> for details on the model hyperparameters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Background Changes</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider different background changes and a moving distractor (see Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Background Changes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) that alter the visual appearance of the scene while preserving the underlying transition dynamics. These changes are applied only at test time, unless otherwise stated, and are designed to isolate the effect of slow features on the planning performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/backgrounds_pm.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/84;" width="476" height="84" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>The six different scenarios that we use to measure robustness based on PointMaze with checkerboard background. From left to right, these are: <span id="S5.F4.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NC</span>: No Change, <span id="S5.F4.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SC</span>: Slight background Change , <span id="S5.F4.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>: Color gradient background, <span id="S5.F4.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LC</span>: Large Color background Change, <span id="S5.F4.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LCG</span>: Large Color Gradient background change, and <span id="S5.F4.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>: moving Distractors with yellow and magenta dots.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Results</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.4 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the success rate for the PointMaze task under background changes and a moving distractor. Results for PointMaze correspond to models trained for <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> epochs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness to the background.</span> We note that DINO-WM displays degradation in performance when the visual background is different from the one seen when training (NC). For instance, in the PointMaze task, while DINO-WM achieves <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8</annotation></semantics></math> success rate under NC, its performance drops for SC, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.72" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.72</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.72</annotation></semantics></math>, and it drops even more under aggressive changes, such as LCG, achieving <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.48</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.48</annotation></semantics></math> success rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, our model consistently achieves high success rates across background changes in PointMaze (around <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.76</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.76</annotation></semantics></math> success). This highlights that invariance with the bisimulation encoder effectively “filters out” background-dependent features from the latent dynamics, leading to reliable planning despite significant visual changes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with DR.</span> Domain randomization performs well when test-time backgrounds resemble combinations of visual changes observed during training (<math id="S5.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.82" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.82</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.82</annotation></semantics></math> success rate for NC, SC, and C). However, its performance degrades substantially under an aggressive background change (LCG) that are not covered by the randomized training distribution, i.e., achieving <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.64</annotation></semantics></math> success rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Moving distractor.</span> Under the moving distractor, DINO-WM again has its performance dropped, indicating that persistent but task-irrelevant motion in the background can also dominate the learned latent dynamics. Our model remains consistent, as the distractor does not affect the transition dynamics and is then suppressed by the bisimulation encoder.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Success rate of DINO-Bisim under different scenarios (Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Background Changes ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) compared to DINO-WM with and without DR.</figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>On Different Pretrained Visual Encoders</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.5 On Different Pretrained Visual Encoders ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports the success rate achieved by our model when using different pretrained visual encoders. We observe that training the model <em id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">end-to-end</em> without DINOv2 features results in a clear degradation in performance (e.g., a success rate of <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.26</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.26</annotation></semantics></math> under LC) compared to training with DINOv2 (<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.86</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.86</annotation></semantics></math> success rate under LC). This behavior is expected, as learning accurate latent transition dynamics relies on sufficiently informative visual representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate robustness using SimDINOv2 and iBOT features. SimDINOv2 (with ViT-B/16) produces patch embeddings of higher dimensionality than DINOv2 (768 compared to the 384 of DINOv2). As all models are trained with the same number of samples, the larger feature dimensionality may lead to a lower success rate (for example due to overfitting). Nevertheless, performance remains consistent across background changes, indicating that our bisimulation encoder continues to suppress task-irrelevant visual features coming from SimDINOv2 embeddings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, with iBOT features our model achieves strong planning performance (around <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.72" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.72</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.72</annotation></semantics></math> success rate) and robustness comparable to the model with DINOv2, further indicating that the proposed approach generalizes to different pretrained visual encoders.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>On the Reward-aware Bisimulation Encoder</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work on bisimulation-based MPC incorporates an explicit reward predictor as part of the bisimulation objective to estimate rewards for planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite> (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>). While such a design is important for value approximation or policy transfer, it is not fundamental for our JEPA. Here the goal is to learn an invariant latent representation that preserves control-relevant transition dynamics rather than task-specific reward structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, when a reward predictor is included, Figure <a href="#A1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A.6 Reward-aware Bisimulation Encoder: Training Metrics ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows that the reward distance converges to near zero early in training and provides little additional signal for improving accuracy in the transition dynamics. This suggests that, for the PointMaze task, reward prediction does not contribute beyond what is already captured by the transition dynamics.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussions and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that DINO-WM is not robust under background changes and distractors. By enforcing control-relevant invariance via bisimulation on top of pretrained visual features, we obtain latent embeddings <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower-dimensional than that of DINO-WM that are robust for planning under visual shifts, without reward supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We note two key limitations of our work: <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1)</annotation></semantics></math> we assume access to sufficiently informative pretrained visual features. While we show robustness across different self-supervised encoders (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.5 On Different Pretrained Visual Encoders ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), performance degrades when the visual representations lack semantic structure (i.e., without DINOv2), indicating that bisimulation-based invariance cannot compensate for poor visual features. <math id="S6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2)</annotation></semantics></math> Our theoretical analysis focuses on reward-free bisimulation with goal-reaching costs and yields a horizon-dependent bound. While this aligns with JEPAs, it yields looser bounds than its reward-aware counterpart. Understanding whether <math id="S6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(T)</annotation></semantics></math> is fundamental remains open.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several directions come naturally from this work. First, we can integrate the bisimulation encoder in gradient-based planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parthasarathy et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which may benefit from smoother and invariant latent dynamics. Another direction is to combine the bisimulation invariance with adaptive policies, enabling online refinement of the invariant representation as the agent encounters new visual conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">From a theoretical perspective, extending our analysis to reward-aware bisimulation could clarify the trade-offs between JEPAs’ modularity and tighter generalization bounds. Finally, considering complex manipulation tasks and long-horizon planning problems is under current implementation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work aims to advance robust, task-agnostic visual world models for planning by improving representation learning under visual distribution shifts. There are many potential societal impacts of this work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix provides additional details that complement the main text. We include specifics on the architecture and implementation of the proposed bisimulation encoder and transition model, further discussion of the PCA-based variance-covariance regularization, and extended descriptions of the experimental setup, including task configurations, domain randomization, and planning details. We also provide the proofs for the generalization bound in Section <a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Model Architecture</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides additional details on the architecture of the proposed joint-embedding predictive world model with bisimulation encoder.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.1 </span>Overview</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The DINO-Bisim model takes visual observations, proprioceptive inputs, and actions at the current timestep and predicts the next bisimulation latent state, along with an optional reward prediction. Visual observations are encoded using a pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 visual encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, followed by a bisimulation encoder implemented as an MLP to produce the latent state. Proprioceptive inputs and actions are embedded using lightweight 1D convolutional encoders. The resulting embeddings are concatenated and processed by a 6-layer transformer to predict the next bisimulation latent state. A separate reward MLP predicts the reward from the latent state, however, this component is not used in our experiments, as discussed in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and throughout the main text.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/System_Architecture.png" id="A1.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/159;" width="476" height="159" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Overview of the DINO-Bisim architecture.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.2 </span>Bisimulation Memory Buffer (Replay Buffer)</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recalling the definition of the bisimulation metric introduced in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Bisimulation Metric ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> and in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro, 2020</a>)</cite>, the corresponding loss involves computing differences between selected pairs of states. Since a single training iteration can only leverage the current batch of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> states, we introduce a bisimulation memory buffer that stores up to <math id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1000</annotation></semantics></math> previously generated states, also following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. This buffer allows comparisons with a larger and more diverse set of past states, thereby improving the stability and effectiveness of the bisimulation representation learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.3 </span>Patch design in Bisimulation Model</h4>

<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/Dino-Bisim-Architecture.png" id="A1.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Bisimulation encoder with patch-based design, with <math id="A1.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>196</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196</annotation></semantics></math> of patches and <math id="A1.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> output patch dimension.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Why Patch-based Design?</span> The bisimulation model adopts a patch-based design, in which visual inputs are partitioned into spatial patches and each patch is encoded independently. This design builds upon the bisimulation encoder in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite> and naturally aligns with the output format of DINOv2 and other patch-based visual encoders. Beyond architectural compatibility, the patch-based formulation substantially reduces the number of trainable parameters, leading to a more compact and efficient model while empirically improving performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More concretely, an example architecture using the hyperparameters in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ A.1.4 Hyperparameters ‣ A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> is illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.1.3 Patch design in Bisimulation Model ‣ A.1 Model Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Rather than flattening a feature map of size <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14\times 14\times 384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>384</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14\times 14\times 384</annotation></semantics></math> into a <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75264" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>75264</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75264</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector as input to the first layer, the patch-based bisimulation encoder performs <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>196</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196</annotation></semantics></math> parallel forward passes using a shared MLP whose input dimension is <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>384</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">384</annotation></semantics></math>. As a result, the number of parameters in the first layer is reduced from <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(75,264\times 256)+256=19,267,840" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>75,264</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>19,267,840</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(75,264\times 256)+256=19,267,840</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(384\times 256)+256=98,560" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>384</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>98,560</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(384\times 256)+256=98,560</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math> is the hidden layer dimension, with only negligible additional overhead from the spatial embedding parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latent Space Dimensionality Comparison.</span> DINO-WM operates on patch-based visual representations produced by DINOv2, consisting of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>196</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196</annotation></semantics></math> patches with <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>384</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">384</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embeddings each, resulting in a latent representation of size <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196\times 384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>196</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>384</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196\times 384</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, our patch-based bisimulation encoder preserves the same spatial structure but maps each patch to a low-dimensional latent embedding. This yields a representation of size <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196\times 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>196</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196\times 32</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, our model operates in a latent space that is more than <math id="A1.SS1.SSS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller than that of DINO-WM, while maintaining improved robustness to slow, task-irrelevant features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.4 </span>Hyperparameters</h4>

</div>
