<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We list below the main hyperparameters used by the bisimulation encoder and transition model. These parameters control the dimensionality of the latent representation, the size of the comparison set used for bisimulation representation learning, and the dimensionality of visual and action embeddings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bisimulation Memory Buffer Size and Comparison Size.</span>
The capacity of the bisimulation memory buffer and the number of stored latent states used for pairwise comparisons when computing the bisimulation loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action Dimension (<span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">action_dim</span>).</span>
The dimensionality of the encoded action representation, used as input to the reward predictor that is not in use for our experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of Patches (<span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">num_patches</span>).</span>
The number of spatial patches output by the bisimulation encoder, matching the patch decomposition of the visual pretrained encoder.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latent Dimension (<span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">latent_dim</span>).</span>
The dimensionality of the bisimulation latent space for each patch.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patch Dimension (<span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">patch_dim</span>).</span>
The dimensionality of each patch embedding produced by the bisimulation encoder; in our implementation, this is set equal to <span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">latent_dim</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patch Embedding Dimension (<span id="A1.SS1.SSS4.p8.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">patch_emb_dim</span>).</span>
The dimensionality of the input patch embeddings provided by the pretrained visual encoder, matching the output dimension of DINOv2.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span> Our experiments use DINOv2, SimDINOv2 and iBOT as pretrained visual encoder, which encode background appearance along the dominant principal components (see Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>). As noted in the DINOv2 paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, background information can be attenuated by thresholding the first principal component. Consistent with this observation and our illustration in Figures <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.2 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we make the preliminary assessment that task-irrelevant appearance factors predominantly align with the first principal component direction in the latent feature space.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method.</span> The bisimulation encoder is initialized with random parameters and is first trained using the standard VICReg objective for a small number of epochs to stabilize representation learning. We then perform a one-time principal component analysis to identify the dominant direction associated with task-irrelevant variation. After a number of warm-up epochs, we replace the standard VICReg loss with the proposed PCA-based VICReg objective, which helps to suppresses variance along the identified principal component directions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">An example training run with a vectorized bisimulation latent representation of dimension <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="196\times 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>196</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">196\times 32</annotation></semantics></math> (corresponding to the number of patches and per-patch latent dimensionality), where PCA-based VICReg is enabled after <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math> epochs, is shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A.2 PCA-based Variance Covariance Regularization ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Result.</span> While this staged regularization approach improves the stability of invariant representation learning, we hypothesize that a tighter integration of PCA-based regularization throughout training and planning, rather than a discrete loss swap, could further enhance invariance. Exploring such joint objectives is an interesting direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/PCA_Loss.png" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/182;" width="476" height="182" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>First two principal components (PCs) of three distinct states (colors) observed under three different backgrounds (marker shapes) for the PointMaze task. The goal of the bisimulation encoder is to map identical states across backgrounds to nearby latent representations. <span id="A1.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left.</span> DINOv2 embeddings <math id="A1.F7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> show strong separation along the first PC for identical states under different backgrounds, indicating that background variation dominates the leading principal direction. <span id="A1.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Middle.</span> Bisimulation embeddings <math id="A1.F7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=h_{\eta}(z_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=h_{\eta}(z_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> after 50 epochs with standard VICReg still exhibit separation along the first PC, preserving background-dependent variation. <span id="A1.F7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right.</span> Bisimulation embeddings after 90 epochs with PCA-based VICReg (activated at epoch 50) show improved clustering of identical states across backgrounds, consistent with suppression of task-irrelevant variation.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/PCA_background_appendix.png" id="A1.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/158;" width="476" height="158" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>First twp principal components (PC1 and PC2) of latent embeddings produced by DINOv2, SimDINOv2, and iBOT for a PointMaze observation. In all cases, PC1 captures a large percentage of the total variance that predominantly encodes background and layout information rather than control-relevant features.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Additional Information on the Navigation Task</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides additional details on the simple navigation task used in our experiments, complementing the high-level description in the main text.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/PointMazeTask.png" id="A1.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/68;" width="476" height="68" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>PointMaze task, from leftmost the initial state to the rightmost the goal state</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">PointMaze <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2020</a>)</cite> is a force-actuated 2-DoF navigation environment in which a ball moves in the Cartesian <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> plane with the objective of reaching a target location. The agent observes proprioceptive state information and evolves under continuous dynamics that capture velocity, acceleration, and inertia. For a fair comparison, we train all models on <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2000</annotation></semantics></math> fully random trajectories, matching the data setup in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. See Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A.3 Additional Information on the Navigation Task ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> for a sequence of frames that illustrates the planning from an initial state to a goal state.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Planning</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We optimize the action sequence using CEM. At each step, CEM samples multiple candidate action sequences, rolls them out using the learned model, selects the sequences with lowest cost (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.5 Planning ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), and updates the sampling distribution accordingly. The first action of the optimized sequence is played, and the process repeats with a receding horizon.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although gradient-based planning methods have recently been proposed and validated in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parthasarathy et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for DINO-WM, we focus on CEM for fair comparison with DINO-WM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Domain Randomization for the PointMaze Task</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate robustness through data augmentation, we apply domain randomization to the PointMaze task by modifying the visual appearance of the environment during training. In particular, <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the training data are rendered with randomized visual backgrounds, while the remaining trajectories retain the default appearance. The randomization includes background color changes and gradient-based background modifications, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ A.5 Domain Randomization for the PointMaze Task ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid introducing spurious temporal artifacts that could make the transition dynamics learning harder, the randomized background is kept fixed within each trajectory but varies across different trajectories. Importantly, these visual modifications do not alter the underlying environment dynamics, agent behavior, or goal locations, ensuring that domain randomization affects only task-irrelevant visual features.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/backgrounds_DR.png" id="A1.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/203;" width="476" height="203" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Examples of domain-randomized visual observations for the PointMaze task. During training, background appearance is randomized across trajectories using color shifts, gradient backgrounds, and fixed distractors (i.e., the dot outside the maze) while the underlying maze layout and transition dynamics remain unchanged.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.6 </span>Reward-aware Bisimulation Encoder: Training Metrics</h3>

<div id="A1.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let us now analyze the training dynamics of the reward-aware bisimulation encoder to assess the contribution of the reward prediction term relative to the transition-based objectives. Following prior work on bisimulation-based MPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shimizu and Tomizuka, 2025</a>)</cite>, we include an auxiliary reward predictor during training, although it is not used for training nor planning in our experiments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F11" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/training_loss.png" id="A1.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/113;" width="238" height="113" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Training losses value versus the training epochs.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A.6 Reward-aware Bisimulation Encoder: Training Metrics ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reports the evolution of the main loss components throughout training. We observe that the reward prediction loss rapidly converges to near zero early in training and remains negligible afterwards. This indicates that, for the navigation task considered, reward prediction provides little additional learning signal beyond what is already captured by the transition dynamics. As a result, the reward term has a negligible influence on the learned latent representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, the transition losses and representation regularization terms (including the VICReg and bisimulation objectives) remain active throughout training and dominate the optimization process. These components are responsible for making the latent space to preserve control-relevant dynamics while suppressing task-irrelevant visual features. This empirical observation supports the design choice adopted in the main experiments, where we drop the reward prediction term and rely only on transition-based bisimulation to enforce invariance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.7 </span>Moving Distractors</h3>

<div id="A1.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate robustness to dynamic but task-irrelevant visual variations, we consider two moving distractors in the PointMaze task. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ A.5 Domain Randomization for the PointMaze Task ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we augment the environment with colored distractor objects (yellow and magenta dots) that move continuously within the maze while remaining decoupled from the agent dynamics and task objectives.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The distractors introduce persistent motion that can dominate DINO-WM latent dynamics, despite being irrelevant for control. On the other hand our bisimulation-based representation is designed to suppress such task-irrelevant motion by enforcing equivalence between states that exhibit identical on-policy transition behavior. As a result, planning performance remains stable in the presence of moving distractors, whereas DINO-WM tend to drop in performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18639v1/figures/moving_distractor_appendix.png" id="A1.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/83;" width="476" height="83" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Moving distractor setting in PointMaze. Yellow and magenta dots move continuously within the maze, introducing dynamic but task-irrelevant visual variation while preserving the underlying transition dynamics.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.8 </span>Reward-Free Generalization Bound: Proof of Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1 (Reward-free planning generalization bound). ‣ 4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a></h3>

<div id="A1.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first provide an auxiliary lemma regarding the 1-Wasserstein distance which we use in the proof of Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1 (Reward-free planning generalization bound). ‣ 4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma A.1</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Villani and others, 2008</a>)</cite>)<span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu,\text{ and }\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> and </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu,\text{ and }\nu</annotation></semantics></math> be two probability measures on the metric space <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\Omega,d_{\pi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\Omega,d_{\pi})</annotation></semantics></math>, then</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle W_{1}(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\|f\|_{L}\leq 1}\left(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}[f(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\nu}[f(y)]\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ν</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0.1389em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">sup</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle W_{1}(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{\|f\|_{L}\leq 1}\left(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}[f(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\nu}[f(y)]\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Lipschitz norm (i.e., <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|f\|_{L}\leq\sup_{x\neq y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.1389em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">sup</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|f\|_{L}\leq\sup_{x\neq y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|}</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We will later invoke the auxiliary result above in the proofs of Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1 (Reward-free planning generalization bound). ‣ 4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>. To make this step explicit, we first show how the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality implies a
Lipschitz-based bound on differences of expectations. Let <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mu\triangleq P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),\text{ and }\nu\triangleq P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>≜</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext> and </mtext><mi>ν</mi><mo>≜</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\triangleq P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),\text{ and }\nu\triangleq P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime}),</annotation></semantics></math> be two probability measures on the metric space <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\Omega,d_{\pi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\Omega,d_{\pi})</annotation></semantics></math>, and define a scalar-valued function <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s(\tilde{z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(\tilde{z})</annotation></semantics></math> on the latent space <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>. Assuming that <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(z)</annotation></semantics></math> is a <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz with respect to <math id="A1.SS8.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e.,</p>

<div id="A1.SS8.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS8.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS8.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proof of Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1 (Reward-free planning generalization bound). ‣ 4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>:</span>
We begin the proof by first noticing that the goal-reaching cost used for planning is Lipschitz on the bounded set of bisimulation latent states, i.e., <math id="A1.SS8.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{w:\|w\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{w:\|w\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Indeed, for any <math id="A1.SS8.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w,w^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w,w^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A1.SS8.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|w\|_{2},\|w^{\prime}\|_{2},\|w_{g}\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|w\|_{2},\|w^{\prime}\|_{2},\|w_{g}\|_{2}\leq{H}_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have the following expression</p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left|c(w)-c(w^{\prime})\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left|c(w)-c(w^{\prime})\right|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\left|\|w-w_{g}\|_{2}^{2}-\|w^{\prime}-w_{g}\|_{2}^{2}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\left|\|w-w_{g}\|_{2}^{2}-\|w^{\prime}-w_{g}\|_{2}^{2}\right|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>

</table>
<p id="A1.SS8.p5.2" class="ltx_p">so <math id="A1.SS8.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c(w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(w)</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A1.SS8.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4{H}_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4{H}_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We further write the recursion</p>

<p id="A1.SS8.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where we assume that <math id="A1.SS8.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{\pi}_{0}(z)\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{\pi}_{0}(z)\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We then prove by induction that <math id="A1.SS8.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{\pi}_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{\pi}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A1.SS8.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz with respect to <math id="A1.SS8.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A1.SS8.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T}\triangleq 8{H}_{w}T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}\triangleq 8{H}_{w}T</annotation></semantics></math>, which implies (<span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p8.1" class="ltx_p">For <math id="A1.SS8.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0</annotation></semantics></math> it holds trivially. Assume it holds for <math id="A1.SS8.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T-1</annotation></semantics></math>. Then for any <math id="A1.SS8.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z,z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z,z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>

</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Note that the first term is bounded by the quantity <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4{H}_{w}\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4{H}_{w}\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. On the other hand, for the second term, since <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{\pi}_{T-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>π</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{\pi}_{T-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T-1}</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz with respect to <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>, we can use Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality to bound <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\left|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{z}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z)}J^{\pi}_{T-1}(\tilde{z})-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{z}^{\prime}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})}J^{\pi}_{T-1}(\tilde{z}^{\prime})\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∼</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∼</mo><mi>P</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>π</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{z}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z)}J^{\pi}_{T-1}(\tilde{z})-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{z}^{\prime}\sim P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})}J^{\pi}_{T-1}(\tilde{z}^{\prime})\right|</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="A1.SS8.p9.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="L_{T-1}W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T-1}W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right),</annotation></semantics></math> i.e., by using (<a href="#A1.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ A.8 Reward-Free Generalization Bound: Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Using the definition of the bisimulation metric, with the reward term dropped, we have
<math id="A1.SS8.p10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right)=\gamma^{-1}d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{1}\left(P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z),P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid z^{\prime})\right)=\gamma^{-1}d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, we obtain</p>
<table id="A1.EGx15" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex19"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left|J^{\pi}_{T}(z)-J^{\pi}_{T}(z^{\prime})\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left|J^{\pi}_{T}(z)-J^{\pi}_{T}(z^{\prime})\right|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex19.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leq 4{H}_{w}\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}+L_{T-1}d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\leq 4{H}_{w}\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}+L_{T-1}d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p11.1" class="ltx_p">As we assume that <math id="A1.SS8.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})+\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|h_{\eta}(z)-h_{\eta}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})+\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, then</p>
<table id="A1.EGx16" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E8"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left|J^{\pi}_{T}(z)-J^{\pi}_{T}(z^{\prime})\right|\leq\left(4{H}_{w}+L_{T-1}\right)d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})+4{H}_{w}\varepsilon." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>π</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left|J^{\pi}_{T}(z)-J^{\pi}_{T}(z^{\prime})\right|\leq\left(4{H}_{w}+L_{T-1}\right)d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})+4{H}_{w}\varepsilon.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS8.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Unrolling the recursion and assuming that <math id="A1.SS8.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is sufficiently small, i.e., <math id="A1.SS8.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\leq d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\leq d_{\pi}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="A1.SS8.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T}\triangleq 8{H}_{w}T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}\triangleq 8{H}_{w}T</annotation></semantics></math>, which implies the bound as stated in Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 4.1 (Reward-free planning generalization bound). ‣ 4.6 A Generalization Bound ‣ 4 Our World Model ‣ Learning Invariant Visual Representations for Planning withJoint-Embedding Predictive World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
